svg.title: Stage 1B lab: actual nesting layers from physical CPU to the L3 test VM
svg.desc: Physical CPU, Windows host OS, VMware Workstation (L0), nested ESXi (L1), kvm-learning-01 Ubuntu guest (L2) with Linux KVM and QEMU, and the nested test VM (L3). Right panel shows the VM-exit path and measured timings.
svg.text: kvm-learning-01: the real nesting chain in this lab (OBSERVED 2026-09-27)
L3
Nested test VM (disposable, direct kernel boot)
Ubuntu kernel 6.8.0-142 + busybox initramfs; 1 vCPU, 256 MiB
virtio-blk -> vda, virtio-scsi -> sda, virtio-net -> eth0
dmesg: "Hypervisor detected: KVM", clocksource kvm-clock
also defined once through libvirt as domain l3-libvirt-demo
L2
kvm-learning-01: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS guest of ESXi, 192.168.50.30
2 vCPU, 4 GiB, 40 GB thin disk on PVSCSI, one VMXNET3 NIC on "VM Network", UEFI
sees CPU flags vmx + ept + unrestricted_guest because ESXi VM has vhv.enable = TRUE
User space: QEMU 8.2.2 process (qemu-system-x86_64)
vCPU thread "CPU 0/KVM"; device models (virtio, q35, SeaBIOS)
started directly, or by libvirtd 10.0.0 driven by virsh (domain XML)
holds fds: /dev/kvm, anon_inode:kvm-vm, anon_inode:kvm-vcpu
ioctl(KVM_RUN)
Kernel: Linux KVM (kvm + kvm_intel modules) = the L2 hypervisor
/dev/kvm crw-rw---- root:kvm; kvm_intel nested=Y, ept=Y
executes VMLAUNCH/VMRESUME on the VT-x that ESXi presents (virtual VMX)
kvm-ok: "KVM acceleration can be used"
L1
ESXi 8.0.3 VMkernel (esxi-8-lab), guest of Workstation
HV Support = 3; runs kvm-learning-01 in a VMX world, Monitor Mode CPL0
vmware.log: "VMware nested VM support detected", modules hv-vt + gphys-ept
emulates VMX for its guest (VHV) on top of the VMX that Workstation emulates
8 vCPU, 16 GiB; migration-datastore VMFS-6
L0
VMware Workstation Pro 17.6.4 VMM (vmware-vmx), Monitor Mode CPL0
the only hypervisor using the real VT-x/EPT; esxi-8-lab has vhv.enable = TRUE
(if the Windows hypervisor were on, Hyper-V would be L0 and this chain would not work)
host OS
Windows 11 (hypervisorlaunchtype Off)
hosts Workstation; not virtualized itself, so it has no L number
hardware
Intel Core i7-14650HX: physical VT-x + EPT
16 cores / 24 threads, 32 GB RAM
What happens on an L3 VM exit (INFERRED from nested VMX design)
1. L3 traps (I/O, APIC, timer, CPUID, EPT fault ...).
2. The real CPU exits to L0 (Workstation VMM).
3. L0 reflects the exit to L1 (ESXi), which is
emulating VMX for kvm-learning-01.
4. L1 reflects it to L2 (Linux KVM), which handles it,
or returns to QEMU for device emulation.
5. KVM's VMRESUME is itself trapped and emulated by
L1, whose own VMRESUME is emulated by L0.
Consequence (OBSERVED)
Instructions that do not exit run on the real CPU at
near-L2 speed. Every exit costs several hypervisor
round trips, so exit-heavy work (firmware, boot,
device probing) is slow: the full L3 run under KVM
took twice as long as under TCG software emulation.
Measured in Stage 1B (same kernel + initramfs)
Workload
L2 direct
L3 + KVM
L3 + TCG
md5sum 128 MiB
shell loop 300k
QEMU start to exit
Classification
KVM accelerated: YES (CPU 0/KVM thread, /dev/kvm fds,
"Hypervisor detected: KVM" in L3). TCG was run only as a
labeled control. Nested KVM is functional here, but its
exit cost makes this lab unfit for performance numbers.
Wall time includes the workloads; 1 timed run each; indicative only.
Terminology used here (Linux KVM nested-guest convention, extended by one level)
L0 = the hypervisor that runs on the physical CPU. L1 = a guest hypervisor inside an L0 VM. L2 = a VM run by L1; here L2 is itself a hypervisor host (KVM).
L3 = a VM run by the L2 hypervisor. KVM (kernel) and QEMU (user space) together form the L2 hypervisor; they are separate components, not one program.
Windows is the host OS of a type-2 hypervisor and is not itself virtualized, so it is not a level. The CPU hardware is not a level either.
